title: Research Instrument: Types and Examples | AnswerThis
summary: A research instrument is the tool you use to collect data. See six types with examples, how to validate one and how to describe it in Chapter 3.
body_markdown:
A research instrument is the tool you use to collect data for your study. A questionnaire, an interview guide and an observation checklist are all research instruments.


This guide explains the six main types and when to use each. It gives a short sample of every type, then shows how to validate an instrument and how to describe it in Chapter 3.


## TL;DR


-


A research instrument is any tool that collects your data.


-


Choose the type that fits your research questions and your respondents.


-


An instrument can be adopted, adapted or researcher-made.


-


Validate it with expert review, a pilot test and a reliability check.


## What is a research instrument?


A research instrument is what you put in front of your respondents, or what you hold while you observe them. It turns your research questions into data you can analyze.


Each research question needs at least one item or section in the instrument. If a question has no matching item, you will have no data to answer it.


## What are the types of research instruments?


Type


What it collects


Use it when


Questionnaire


Written answers to the same set of questions


You need data from many respondents.


Interview guide


Spoken answers in the participant's own words


You want to understand experiences in depth.


Observation checklist


A record of what people actually do


Behavior matters more than opinion.


Test


Scores that show knowledge or skill


You are measuring learning or ability.


Rating scale or rubric


A rating of quality on set criteria


You are judging a performance or a product.


Document review form


Data taken from records, reports or files


The data already exist in documents.


## Research instrument examples


The samples below are invented for this guide. Each one shows what a small part of the instrument looks like.


### 1. Questionnaire with a Likert scale


Respondents rate each statement from 5 (Strongly agree) to 1 (Strongly disagree).


1.


I set a fixed time for studying every day.


2.


I review my notes before each class.


3.


I finish my assignments before the deadline.


To interpret the mean scores, many theses use a table like this one.


Mean score


Interpretation


4.21 to 5.00


Strongly agree


3.41 to 4.20


Agree


2.61 to 3.40


Neutral


1.81 to 2.60


Disagree


1.00 to 1.80


Strongly disagree


### 2. Interview guide


1.


Can you describe a typical day when you have both work and classes?


2.


What is the hardest part of balancing work and study?


3.


What helps you keep up with your schoolwork?


### 3. Observation checklist


The observer marks Yes or No for each item during one class period.


1.


The teacher states the lesson objective at the start.


2.


Learners work in groups for at least ten minutes.


3.


The teacher checks understanding before the class ends.


### 4. Test


A 30-item multiple-choice test on fractions, given before and after the lessons. Each correct answer earns one point.


### 5. Rating scale or rubric


A rubric for an oral presentation. Each criterion is rated from 4 (Excellent) to 1 (Needs improvement). The criteria are content, organization, delivery and use of visual aids.


### 6. Document review form


A form for reviewing attendance records. It has columns for the month, the number of school days, the number of absences and the stated reason.


## What do adopted, adapted and researcher-made mean?


Kind


What it means


What to do


Adopted


You use an existing instrument without changes.


Cite the source. Ask permission if the owner requires it.


Adapted


You change an existing instrument to fit your study.


Cite the source, say what you changed and validate it again.


Researcher-made


You write the instrument yourself.


Validate it fully before you use it.


Schools have different rules for each kind. Follow your research manual and your adviser.


## How do you validate a research instrument?


1.


Write items that match your research questions. Every item should help answer one question.


2.


Ask experts to review the items. They check whether each item is clear and covers the topic. This is expert validation.


3.


Run a pilot test. Give the instrument to a small group that is similar to your respondents but will not take part in the main study.


4.


Check reliability. For a scale with several items, compute Cronbach's alpha from the pilot data. Then revise or remove weak items.


Many researchers look for a Cronbach's alpha of at least 0.70. The acceptable values range from 0.70 to 0.95 ([Tavakol and Dennick, 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4205511/) ). Use the cut-off your school asks for.


Cronbach's alpha measures internal consistency. It does not show that the instrument is valid. Our guide on[reliability vs validity](https://answerthis.io/blog/reliability-vs-validity) explains the difference.


You can compute the statistic with the AnswerThis[research calculators](https://answerthis.io/research-calculators) . They are free, have no limit on runs and work in your browser. The reliability calculators are Cronbach's alpha, ICC and Cohen's kappa.


## How do you describe the instrument in Chapter 3?


Say what the instrument is, where it came from, what its parts are, how it is scored and how it was validated. Here is a sample paragraph.


*The study used a researcher-made questionnaire with two parts. Part I asked for the respondents' profile. Part II had 20 statements on study habits, rated on a five-point Likert scale from 5 (Strongly agree) to 1 (Strongly disagree). Three experts reviewed the questionnaire for content. It was then pilot tested with 30 students who were not part of the sample, and the Cronbach's alpha was \[value\].*


## What are the most common mistakes?


-


Double-barreled items. “The teacher is clear and friendly” asks two things at once. Split it into two items.


-


Leading questions. “Do you agree that online classes are harmful?” pushes the respondent toward one answer.


-


Items that do not match the research questions. Each item must connect to a question in your statement of the problem.


-


No pilot test. Without one, you find unclear items only after you have collected all your data.

## FAQs


### What is a research instrument in quantitative research?


It is usually a questionnaire, a test or a checklist that gives numbers you can analyze with statistics.


### What is a research instrument in qualitative research?


It is usually an interview guide, a focus group guide or an observation guide. Many qualitative researchers also describe themselves as the main instrument.


### Is a questionnaire the same as a research instrument?


A questionnaire is one type of research instrument. Not every instrument is a questionnaire.


### Do I need permission to use an existing instrument?


Often, yes. Check the terms set by the author or publisher, and always cite the source.


### How many people do I need for a pilot test?


Schools set different numbers. Ask your adviser, and use people who are similar to your respondents but outside your sample.
